newsitem.title: INDIA: Sleepless nights ahead for India equities investors.
newsitem.headline: Sleepless nights ahead for India equities investors.

text.p: Depressed Indian equity markets, dogged by political uncertainties in Uttar Pradesh and New Delhi courtrooms, could be helped by lower interest rates but other would-be rescuers are scarce, analysts told Reuters Thursday.
"I don't see any immediate reasons for the market to pick up in a hurry," Alok Sethi, director at NatWest Markets in Bombay, said, adding that there may be occasional corrections.
In late trading on Thursday, the Bombay Stock Exchange top-30 index at 3127.66 was nearly four percent lower than where it started the month.
Two days ago it was six percent down, but the market underwent a correction during a brief lull in the political buffeting it has suffered almost daily recently.
Sethi listed the politics, a slowing growth, and undistinguished half-year corporate results as negative factors handicapping the market for the rest of the year.
It was hard to find redeeming features, although in terms of market valuations India looked very attractive both historically and regionally, Sethi said.
Some analysts look to expectations that the central bank will cut banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) later this month, which should lower interest rates.
That will benefit both bond and equity markets, HG Asia director Subra Subramanian said.

Meantime political questionmarks stemming from an uncertain outcome to elections this week in Uttar Pradesh, the country's most populous state, and three concurrent corruption trials against former Prime Minister Narasimha Rao weigh on sentiment.
"The political risk factor is the major constraint on the market today. All the other factors are functions of the political situation," Anthony Duckworth, director of research at W.I Carr said.
The country is in need of a stable government with a coherent economic policy to attack the stacking problems of budget deficit and a slowing economy, the analysts agreed.
Bharatiya Janata Party, the main opposition Hindu nationalist party, is almost certain to emerge as the largest single party in Uttar Pradesh, once the results are out on Friday.

But the critical factor for markets will be how any deal struck at the state level between the United Front parties and the Congress/BSP alliance will influence the stability of the central government.

Subramanian said the signs were, with one day of counting to go, that the balance of power within Prime Minister Deve Gowda's 13-party coalition, which depends on Rao's Congress Party's support, will be largely unchanged by the vote.
He also believed that Rao's influence in Congress will fade the longer he is tied up in court, and his ability to threaten a withdrawal from the coalition will diminish correspondingly.
The HG Asia director foresaw the Gowda government surviving until late next year and did not expect the communists and others in the coalition to slow economic reforms significantly.
"The political risk is lower rather than greater,"he said.
Others expressed similar views on the life expectancy of the government, but were less sanguine about effects on sentiment.
"The easy ways of tackling the deficit are getting closed down. The option of raising a lot of money through divestment and cutting expenditure are limited," said Carr's Duckworth.
"Aside from worries about Rao there are more fundamental concerns that keep investors awake at nights," Duckworth said.
